prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Whatever ’tis, whose beauty here below Attracts thee thus and makes thee stream and flow, And wind and curl, and wink and smile, Shifting thy gate and guile; Though thy close commerce nought at all imbars My present search, for eagles eye not stars, And still the lesser by the best And highest good is blest; Yet, seeing all things that subsist and be, Have their commissions from divinity, And teach us duty, I will see What man may learn from thee. First, I am sure, the subject so respected Is well dispos’d, for bodies once infected, Deprav’d, or dead, can have with thee No hold, nor sympathy. Next, there’s in it a restless, pure desire And longing for thy bright and vital fire, Desire that never will be quench’d, Nor can be writh’d, nor wrench’d. These are the magnets which so strongly move And work all night upon thy light and love, As beauteous shapes, we know not why, Command and guide the eye. For where desire, celestial, pure desire Hath taken root, and grows, and doth not tire, There God a commerce states, and sheds His secret on their heads. This is the heart he craves, and who so will But give it him, and grudge not, he shall feel That God is true, as herbs unseen Put on their youth and green.

**The Divine Mirror: On Devotion, Purity, and the Willing Heart**

To understand the fullness of spiritual duty, one must turn an attentive eye toward the natural world. In observing the cosmos—from the steady orbits of the stars to the quiet growth of the earth—it becomes clear that no created thing exists by chance. Every element of nature carries a sacred commission, derived directly from divine authority. The natural order serves as a living testament to its Creator, silently fulfilling its purpose and revealing the fundamental laws that ought to govern the human spirit.

Yet, in contemplating this divine order, a stark truth emerges: light and darkness cannot truly mix. Corrupt, depraved, or spiritually dead entities are fundamentally incompatible with the absolute purity of the Divine. Just as a withered branch cannot draw life from a living vine while remaining detached, a soul mired in moral decay stands alienated from the source of all holiness. Divine purity demands a harmony of nature; that which is spiritually dead possesses no resonance with, nor connection to, the living God.

It follows, then, that true spiritual devotion cannot be defined by superficial ritual or reluctant compliance. Rather, authentic faith is characterized by an unquenchable, steadfast desire for divine light and life. It is an enduring inner flame—a deep, persistent hunger to be aligned with truth and goodness, unaffected by the fleeting distractions or hardships of the mortal world. 

When this celestial desire takes deep root within a person, the Creator does not remain distant. Instead, God establishes a direct, intimate relationship with the soul. To those who cultivate pure intention, He unveils His divine secrets, sharing profound wisdom and spiritual clarity that remain hidden from the worldly and self-absorbed. The receptive heart becomes a sanctuary wherein divine truth is communicated and understood.

Ultimately, the Creator desires neither coerced obedience nor an uninspired sense of obligation. He seeks a willing and ungrudging heart—one that offers itself freely out of love and reverence. To those who surrender their lives into His hands without reservation, God promises complete spiritual renewal and an unfolding revelation of truth, restoring the soul to the vibrant, purposeful existence it was created to enjoy.
outputs.L4:
**The Current of Grace**

To sit beside a mountain stream is to witness a silent, unceasing sermon written in water. Clear, cold, and relentlessly driven, the current carves its path over rugged stone and through tangled roots, refusing ever to settle into the apathy of stagnation. Its clarity is not static; rather, it is maintained by constant motion—a restless purity that casts away impurities precisely because it will not stop moving forward. In observing this unyielding journey toward an unseen ocean, one begins to discern a profound moral and spiritual grammar written into the natural world. Nature, in all its instinctual design, exhibits an innate, irresistible attraction toward Divine Beauty, serving as a living mirror for the human soul.

Humanity, so easily tempted by spiritual lethargy and the allure of static comfort, stands indicted and instructed by the stream’s ceaseless movement. The stream does not question its destination, nor does it allow the obstacles of the terrain to corrupt its clarity. It demonstrates that true purity is not a passive state, but an active, persistent orientation toward the ultimate source of goodness. From this physical phenomenon, we deduce a spiritual truth: the soul’s vitality depends entirely on its refusal to grow still in a world of compromise. Like the water, the human spirit is designed to seek the divine ocean from which it originated, driven by a sacred restlessness that accepts no earthly substitute.

When a soul aligns itself with this natural law—offering an unquenchable, pure devotion that mirrors the stream’s unrelenting flow—the divine response is both profound and transformative. God does not remain a distant observer to such longing. To the heart that remains open, earnest, and continually moving toward Him, He reveals His sacred secrets. These revelations are not loud declarations to the worldly wise, but intimate imparting of spiritual clarity, peace, and wisdom to those whose desire for Him is unadulterated. The continuous pouring out of human devotion creates a vessel capable of receiving the deep, quiet mysteries of God.

Ultimately, this divine interaction culminates in a continuous cycle of spiritual renewal. The stream does not merely run for its own sake; as it flows, it waters the surrounding earth, nourishing life that often goes unnoticed. Heavenly grace operates in much the same manner—subtly, deeply, and without ostentation. Just as subterranean moisture reaches the roots of hidden plants buried in the shadowy underbrush, causing them to quietly regain their vibrant greenness, God’s grace reaches into the obscure, bruised, and weary places of the faithful soul. It is a quiet revitalization. Without dramatic displays or public acclaim, the soul that yields to divine love finds its strength imperceptibly restored, its spirit renewed, and its inner life made fertile once again by the living waters of grace.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 17th-century metaphysical poem about a flowing river and spiritual devotion.
counterfactuals.output:
**The River’s Motion, and the Soul’s Devotion**

Mark how this liquid Pilgrim cuts its way,
Unwearied through the labyrinths of clay;
Though born of clouds, by Heaven’s soft weeping bred,
It scorns the quiet of its mountain bed.
No flow’ry bank can bribe its course to stay,
Nor shaded grove tempt its swift feet delay;
It hastes away, with pure, unbidden zeal,
Till in the distant Sea its heart it heal.

O strange Hydro-geometry of Grace!
The lower still it glides, the higher runs its race:
By stooping down to valley’s lowest dust,
It climbs the Ocean of the Only Just.
For by a holy gravitation led,
It seeks no height, but takes the lowest bed,
And in that lowliness finds power to move
Straight to the abyss of everlasting Love.

Even so my Soul, a tide of native breath,
Winds through the narrow channels of this Death.
Yet, ah! Too oft my troubled current strays,
Choked with the silt of worldly, winding ways;
I mirror earth, and forget the pristine skies,
While in my depths the heavy sediment lies.
Break down these banks of self! Lord, let Thy Grace
Sweep through my depths, and all my filth erase.

Absorb my little Drop into Thy Sea,
That I no more may be myself, but Thee!
As rivers lose their names within the Main,
And dying to their streams, true boundless Life regain,
So let my finite currents cease to flow,
And drown my Will in Thine, above, below:
For to be swallowed in Thy vast Abyss,
Is not to drown, but to be crowned in Bliss.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a devotional poem in the style of Henry Vaughan. Address a stream or river, observing its movement and drawing a spiritual lesson about celestial desire, divine communion, and a heart seeking God.
counterfactuals.output:
Fair, crystal stream, whose liquid race
Hath never learned a sluggish pace,
Thou silent runner of the glade,
Unmoved by earthly sun or shade!
Through darksome vales and stony tracks
Thy pure, unwearied glass reflects
The quiet stars, the azure sky,
And beauty of the realm on high.

Thou well remember’st thy high birth,
Born far above this lower earth,
Where cloud and dew from heaven did fall
To shape thy sacred fountain-call;
And now, though winding deep and low,
Thy steadfast waters onward flow,
Seeking with an unquenched desire
The distant Ocean of thy Sire.

Ah, foolish heart! how cold and slow
Do my poor, earthy passions flow!
I linger in the fleeting dust,
A prey to shadow, doubt, and lust;
While this bright brook, devoid of sin,
Bears heaven’s glorious image in,
And hastes to join the boundless Sea,
The emblem of Eternity.

O sacred Wave! teach me to glide
Unstained through time’s polluted tide;
Though wild-briers pull, and banks entreat,
Let me not stay my eager feet,
But keep my celestial eye
Fixed on the fountain-head on high,
That every drop of life may be
A silver path that leads to Thee.

Lord, touch this dry and barren ground,
Where only weeds of care are found;
Turn my faint spirit to a spring
That doth Thy praise unceasing sing;
Till, merged within Thy light divine,
My stream of life is lost in Thine!
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Please give me a classic metaphysical poem that uses a river's flow as a metaphor for divine grace and the pure longing of the soul.
counterfactuals.output:
One of the finest classic metaphysical poems on this theme is **"The Waterfall"** by the 17th-century Welsh poet **Henry Vaughan** (published in his collection *Silex Scintillans* in 1655). 

In true Metaphysical fashion, Vaughan uses an extended conceit (an elaborate metaphor): he gazes at a river rushing over a waterfall and sees in its movement the passage of human life, the cleansing power of divine grace, and the soul's ultimate yearning to return to the infinite "ocean" of God.

***

### **The Waterfall**
*by Henry Vaughan (1621–1695)*

With what deep murmurs through time’s silent stealth
Doth thy transparent, cool, and shadowy stream
Make upwards haste to strive with sun and beam,
And by a fatal, inbred force still slide
Downwards, to be more pure and sanctified!

Fair stream! where the sun prints his beams,
And plays the various shapes of dreams,
Ah! what is human life, but such
A stream, that glides and falls as much?
Yet water, though it fall so low,
Doth from its original flow
Rise up again, and by its fall
Gain strength to ascend, and conquer all.

O sovereign water! which when God
First spake, didst feel His quick’ning rod,
And was the first of all the earth
That had a spirit and a birth:
Unless that Spirit, which did move
Upon thy waters, did improve
Thy native force, and make thee rise
Beyond the reach of earthly eyes,
Thou hadst been still a sluggish pool,
Dull, heavy, cold, and dark, and cool.

But now, by virtue of that grace,
Thou runn’st a bright, eternal race,
And leaving all thy dross behind,
Doth seek the Ocean of the Mind,
Where every drop at last shall be
Merged in the great, unmeasured Sea.

Lord! what a pleasant gust this stream has given
My thirsty soul, which roves and sighs for heaven!
Why bold fall thy waters down,
When every drop in thee doth drown
A soul while here? O my invisible estate,
My glorious liberty, still late!
Thou art the channel to that sea
Where all things move, and live, and be.

***

### Key Metaphysical Themes in the Poem:

* **The River as the Soul's Journey:** Vaughan compares human mortality to water falling over a precipice into the abyss. What seems like destruction (death/falling) is actually the means by which the stream is purified.
* **Divine Grace as the Driving Force:** The poet notes that left to itself, water is just a "sluggish pool." It is only through the Holy Spirit moving upon the waters (referencing Genesis) that divine grace imparts motion, guiding the stream back upward toward God.
* **The Soul's Longing (The Ocean):** The river's restless, perpetual flow represents the soul's longing ("my thirsty soul, which roves and sighs for heaven!"). The individual drop of water finds its ultimate peace only when it merges back into the infinite "unmeasured Sea" of the Creator.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
Upon this mossy bank I sit reclined,
To watch the gentle brooklet softly slide;
No earthly tumult here can vex the mind,
Where holy silence governs every tide.
This liquid glass runs pure without delay,
To pay its quiet duty to the day.

Behold how sweetly doth this humble rill
Fulfill the charge its Maker did bestow!
It questions not the High Almighty’s will,
Nor seeks to rise, but still delights to flow.
It teaches man, by gentle, ceaseless course,
To bend his motion to the Heavenly Source.

When unpolluted by the muddy clay,
The water bears the image of the sky;
It captures every golden solar ray,
And holds the light of Providence on high.
So doth the soul, when kept from sin’s disgrace,
Become a mirror for the Father's face.

For as the sunbeam seeks the clearest spring,
To imprint his glory on its glassy breast,
So God’s sweet Grace, on swift, angelic wing,
Doth in the pure and humble bosom rest.
The proud may boast, yet miss the sacred favor,
Which crowns the clean of heart with holy savor.

O Thou, who bad'st this silver stream to run,
Purge Thou my heart of every secret stain!
Direct my thoughts to seek Thy glorious Son,
That I may never flow toward earth in vain.
Make me a brook, though small, yet clear and free,
That in my depths the world Thy Light may see.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in archaic English where the speaker talks to a river, comparing its restless motion to the soul's desire for God's light.
counterfactuals.output:
Whither away, O swift and silver tide,
Dost thou so fiercely cleave the shadowy vale?
No peaceful bower may bid thy waves abide,
Though evening fall, and starry lamps turn pale.

Thou hast no slumber in thy stony bed,
Nor turn’st aside to kiss the flowering shore;
By some unslaked, divine compulsion led,
Thou seek’st the boundless ocean evermore.

O ceaseless stream! Methinks I see in thee
The image of my spirit’s secret plight:
For as thy foam doth languish for the sea,
So doth my soul pine for God’s holy Light.

Here in this prison-house of mortal clay,
I wander through a dark and fallen sphere;
No earthly pleasure can my heart delay,
No transient fountain quench my longing here.

Unquiet river, racing through the gloom,
Thou wilt not rest till in the deep thou art;
And I, a pilgrim hastening to my doom,
Bear in my breast an all-unquiet heart.

Flow on, clear flood! Seek thou thy vast abyss,
And teach my trembling soul her course to run,
Till, loosed from earth, she drown in sacred bliss,
And rest forever in the Heavenly Sun.
